title: They didn’t just reject the message.
paragraphs: They didn’t just reject the message.

They cut it.
Piece… by piece…
And fed it to the fire.
Sit with that.
Jeremiah 36 is not a calm chapter. It is a collision—between heaven’s voice and human pride, between warning and rebellion, between mercy and a man who thinks he can silence God.

God speaks.
That alone is mercy.
He tells Jeremiah: “Write all the words I have spoken… perhaps they will turn… and I will forgive.” (Jeremiah 36:2–3, paraphrased)
Did you catch that?
Judgment is coming—but mercy is still reaching.
So the prophet calls for a scribe.
Baruch.

Not the headline name.
Not the fiery preacher.
But the steady hand.

He sits.
Scroll open.
Ink ready.
Heart trembling.
And he writes.

Every warning.
Every plea.
Every coming consequence.

He doesn’t dilute it.
He doesn’t soften it.
He doesn’t protect people’s feelings at the expense of God’s truth.
He writes what God said.
Faithfully.
Then comes the moment.
Baruch stands before the people and reads the scroll aloud. The atmosphere tightens. You can almost feel the air get heavy. Conviction is in the room. Some are afraid. Some are shaken.
But fear of God is not the same as surrender to God.
The scroll is brought to the king—Jehoiakim.

Powerful.
Untouchable.
Comfortable in sin.
As the words are read, something inside him resists. Not confusion—rebellion. Not ignorance—defiance.
He takes a knife.
And here is the horror:
Every few columns… he slices the scroll… and throws it into the fire.

Slowly.
Deliberately.
Without trembling.

No fear of God.
No repentance.
No humility.
Just control.
As if destroying the scroll could erase the truth.
As if burning the warning could cancel the coming judgment.
This is the anatomy of sin.

We don’t just ignore God’s Word.
We try to edit it.
We cut the parts that confront us.
We silence the parts that expose us.

“Don’t talk about sin.”
“Don’t mention judgment.”
“Don’t call me to repent.”
Slice.
Burn.
Repeat.
But here is the holy interruption:
God is not threatened by human rejection.
After the scroll is burned… God speaks again.
“Take another scroll… and write all the former words again.” (Jeremiah 36:28)
Again.
Let that sink in.

They rejected Him—He speaks again.
They burned His Word—He sends it again.
They hardened their hearts—He extends mercy again.
This is not weakness.
This is stubborn grace.
And Baruch?
He picks up the pen again.

No bitterness.
No quitting.
No compromise.
He writes again.

Faithfulness is not proven when people applaud you.
It is proven when people reject what you carry—and you still carry it.
Listen closely:
Some of you are Baruch.

You’re not the loudest voice.
You’re not the platform personality.
But you’ve been entrusted with truth.

In your home.
In your workplace.
In your quiet obedience.
Do not edit the Word to be accepted.

Write it.
Speak it.
Live it.
Faithfully.
But this story doesn’t end in Jeremiah’s time.
It points forward.
Because humanity didn’t stop at burning scrolls.
We rejected the Living Word.
Jesus Christ came—full of grace and truth (John 1:14). He didn’t just speak God’s Word—He is the Word made flesh (John 1:1).
And what did we do?
We didn’t take a knife to parchment.
We nailed Him to a cross.

We cut Him off.
We cast Him out.
We tried to silence Him forever.
But here is the victory that shakes history:

You cannot burn what God has ordained to live.
You cannot bury what heaven has declared victorious.
On the third day—He rose.

Alive.
Unstoppable.
Glorious.
That is the Gospel.
We are not just Baruch in the story.
We are Jehoiakim.

We resist truth.
We protect sin.
We try to control God instead of surrender to Him.
But grace steps in.

Jesus takes the judgment we deserve.
He bears our sin.
He dies in our place.
And He rises to offer us life.
Forgiveness is not earned—it is received.
But it requires something Jehoiakim refused:
Repentance.
So here’s the question that will not leave you alone:
When God’s Word confronts you…

Will you cut it?
Or will you let it cut you?
One path hardens your heart.
The other saves your soul.
Don’t burn the Word that came to rescue you.
Come to Christ.

Turn from sin.
Trust in Him alone.
And experience the mercy that keeps speaking—even when you’ve been running.
Because even now…
God is still writing.

Still calling.
Still saving.
And this time…
Don’t throw it in the fire.
“The word of our God will stand forever.” — Isaiah 40:8
Someone out there is still holding the knife… and grace is reaching for them.
